audience: curious adults with no engineering background
core_question: How does electricity made far away arrive at a wall socket the instant it is needed?
short_answer: Generators make alternating current, transformers raise its voltage for efficient long-distance transmission and lower it again near homes, and operators match supply to demand every second, using frequency as the signal.

key_concepts.name: Generator
key_concepts.explanation: A spinning magnet inside copper coils induces alternating current.
key_concepts.mechanism: The rotor's field sweeps the stator windings, pushing electrons back and forth 60 times a second.
key_concepts.visual_metaphor: A cutaway rotor spinning while a sine wave grows beside it.

key_concepts.name: Step-up transformer
key_concepts.explanation: Raising voltage lowers current for the same power, which cuts line losses.
key_concepts.mechanism: Two windings share an iron core; the turns ratio sets the voltage ratio.
key_concepts.visual_metaphor: Few primary turns, many secondary turns, a voltmeter jumping from 20 kV to 400 kV.

key_concepts.name: Frequency balance
key_concepts.explanation: Grid frequency falls when demand exceeds supply and rises when supply exceeds demand.
key_concepts.mechanism: Extra load brakes every synchronous generator a little, so they all slow together until governors add power.
key_concepts.visual_metaphor: A see-saw of supply and demand driving a frequency needle.

process.detail: Plants turn heat, water or wind into rotation and rotation into AC.
Transformers raise the voltage to hundreds of kilovolts.
High-voltage lines carry power hundreds of kilometers.
Substations and pole transformers lower the voltage for homes.

numbers.fact: Household outlet voltage in North America

misconceptions.myth: Power plants store electricity until you need it.
misconceptions.truth: The grid stores almost nothing; generation must match use moment by moment.

analogies: Frequency is like the speed of a bicycle team riding up and down hills.
